papers.title: FURINA: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Patch Correctness Assessment
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
papers.abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) has made substantial advancements in fixing real-world defects. However, the overfitting problem, namely the phenomenon where APR-generated patches pass the given test suite but fail to correctly fix the underlying defects, remains a major challenge. To mitigate this problem, numerous Automated Patch Correctness Assessment (APCA) methods have been proposed. Among them, learning-based APCA methods currently represent the state-of-the-art (SOTA). However, these methods require training on large, high-quality patch datasets. Moreover, their lack of interpretability, as they often produce only simple binary predictions, provides little support for subsequent manual review. Finally, existing APCA methods often fail to fully leverage the rich contextual information both within and beyond the patched program, and they struggle to incorporate expert knowledge about patch correctness assessment. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising path to address these limitations. Trained on vast corpora, they demonstrate strong generalization across tasks and an ability to learn from experience, allowing them to provide interpretable explanations in a manner analogous to human reasoning. In this paper, we propose a multi-agent framework FURINA, which formulates APCA as a reasoning task. The framework employs a pre-trained retriever and four specialized agents to analyze a candidate patch from multiple perspectives: a Profiler to analyze developer intent from failing tests and bug reports; an Interpreter to analyze code semantics according to the function-level patch; a Critic to analyze potential degradations from the patch context; and a final Judge to synthesize the patches, failing tests, bug reports, intermediate reasoning reports generated by other agents, the retrieved similar patches, along with instructive empirical tips derived from prior APCA studies to determine patch correctness. Evaluation results on the public benchmark CACHE-small demonstrate that FURINA, when equipped with popular LLMs, outperforms SOTA APCA baselines, achieving improvements of at least 5.58% in \(Accuracy\) and 5.93% in \(F1\) . To further assess its reasoning quality, we design a new evaluation scheme that considers three dimensions: factual consistency, logical clarity, and readability. The results show that FURINA achieves a score of at least 4.8 out of 5, demonstrating superior reasoning quality compared with SOTA baselines. Finally, based on our constructed dataset, FURINA still achieves competitive performance, indicating strong generalization ability.

papers.title: Navigating the artificial intelligence frontier on cataloguing and metadata work in libraries: an interview with Getaneh Alemu
papers.abstract: Getaneh Alemu is an experienced Cataloguing and Metadata Librarian with over two decades of experience in higher education and libraries. He specialises in ensuring that metadata is accurate, consistent, usable and standardised. His expertise covers several key metadata standards and tools, including MARC21, MarcEdit, Dublin Core, AACR2, RDA, LCSH, DDC, Alma and Primo. These standards aim to maximise the visibility, discoverability, accessibility and utilisation of library resources.Getaneh has an impressive academic background that includes a PhD in Metadata for Digital Libraries from the University of Portsmouth, earned in 2014. He also holds an MA in Digital Library Learning from Oslo University College, Parma University and Tallinn University, obtained in 2009. Additionally, he earned an MA in Knowledge and Information Management from Ghent University in 2005 and a BA in Library and Information Science from Addis Ababa University in 2001.His research on metadata is well-documented through key publications such as “Metadata Standards and Models” (2024), “The Future of Enriched, Linked, Open and Filtered Metadata” (2022) and “An Emergent Theory of Digital Library Metadata: Enrich then Filter” (2015).Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to automate repetitive, data-intensive and pattern-recognition tasks, thereby freeing human cataloguers for more complex work. What impact will this have?We interviewed Getaneh Alemu because his current work demonstrates a proactive engagement with AI in cataloguing. He is actively involved in exploring, testing and evaluating various AI tools. This exploration extends to discussions with colleagues to understand AI’s practical applications in metadata creation, enrichment and the enhancement of library catalogues and discovery systems.Q1.How does Artificial Intelligence currently impact your work as a cataloguer?Currently, the impact of AI on my cataloguing work is mainly in the exploratory phase. I am actively exploring, testing and evaluating various tools, including the new AI Metadata Assistant from Ex Libris, as well as Copilot, ChatGPT and Gemini. Additionally, I am engaged in ongoing discussions with colleagues in the library to gain a better understanding of the practical applications of these technologies in metadata creation and enrichment, as well as in improving the library catalogue and discovery.We are entering an exciting phase and we must engage as active participants rather than as complainers or passive observers. It’s important to remember that AI is not an external force intruding upon our lives; rather, it is a human innovation that we must use wisely, ethically and responsibly. AI is no longer a distant concept, relegated to the realm of science fiction; it is a reality. The emergence of large language models like ChatGPT and Copilot has made AI increasingly relevant to our work, transforming it from an abstract idea into a practical tool for organising and managing bibliographic data. This process is ongoing and requires continuous learning, critical reflection and experimentation, but is happening at a fast pace.I stay informed about the latest developments in Artificial Intelligence by reading authoritative sources, including “New Horizons in Artificial Intelligence in Libraries” (Balnaves et al., 2025), as well as peer-reviewed journal articles and professional discussions on platforms like LinkedIn. In my workplace, a dedicated team of information librarians regularly updates us on new AI tools and innovations. In this regard, my university shows significant proactivity and remains at the forefront of technological advancement. The university has provided a concise online training module covering the fundamental principles of artificial intelligence, which I have successfully completed.Currently, the impact of AI on my professional responsibilities is limited but overall positive. Although its use is not yet widespread, I am involved in a small-scale experimental project that explores the use of AI-generated metadata for subject headings. We plan to provide further updates as this project progresses.Q2. What are some examples of successful AI implementations in metadata management and cataloguing?We’re observing some promising developments, although they are still in the experimental stages. I utilise the Copilot and Gemini AI tools to check Dewey Decimal numbers and to suggest appropriate subject headings. Ex Libris has introduced an AI assistant called “Metadata Enrichment using AI,” which aids in the ongoing enhancement of bibliographic records. It’s essential to note that Ex Libris emphasises the need for human cataloguers to validate the outputs generated by AI to ensure accuracy and trustworthiness.I tested the AI Assistant with both new and existing records to evaluate its capability to create MARC 21 bibliographic records from minimal input. The tool can handle basic bibliographic elements (such as title and author) or visual sources (like a book cover or an image of the table of contents) and generates a draft record that is sent to the Metadata Editor (MDE).For this test, I supplied an image sourced from a publisher’s website, providing the main title, author and year but deliberately omitting the subtitle. The AI inferred and correctly populated the title along with the subtitle, inserted the correct MARC21 245 field, auto-assigned some basic (generic) subject headings (in the 650 LCSH field) and generated a summary note (520). It also embedded provenance metadata via a note indicating: “Part of the metadata in this record was created with the help of the AI Metadata Assistant.” However, some essential metadata elements were missing such as physical description (300), classification numbers (082 / 050), standard identifier and richer (granular) subject access. ISBD punctuation (e.g. colons, commas) and subfield spacing in 245 and elsewhere were also inconsistent. While effective for generating core descriptive metadata, the Assistant requires cataloguer input to ensure full bibliographic control, structural accuracy and standards compliance.AI has significant potential to improve metadata and cataloguing. While it offers powerful capabilities, integrating AI with existing standards and tools requires effort. AI can enhance metadata, providing users with more intuitive access to information through linked subject systems. Additionally, it can address historical biases in classification systems and improve data quality by conducting consistency checks and detecting anomalies in bibliographic records.Q3.What are your thoughts on the risks and ethical considerations of using AI in metadata and cataloguing?AI-augmented metadata must adhere to established ethical principles by prioritising user-centred access and non-discrimination, reflecting IFLA’s emphasis on “user convenience.” This requires actively addressing the inherent biases present in both AI algorithms and the socio-cultural biases that are built into historical metadata standards. As noted by Gartner (2016) and Bowker and Star (1999), metadata is never completely neutral; every standard and category reflects a particular viewpoint while silencing others. This can result in historical classification schemes that represent colonial perspectives or lack appropriate terminology for diverse cultural expressions.To combat these entrenched biases, it is essential to continuously and critically examine, diversify and decolonise metadata practices to ensure inclusivity and equitable representation.Thus, transparency and accountability in the metadata decisions made by AI are crucial. It is important to highlight the vital role of human oversight and the need for collaborative efforts among all metadata professionals to ensure ethical and responsible information practices.Q4.To what extent can AI automate cataloguing tasks and what tasks are best suited for automation?AI holds significant potential to automate various cataloguing tasks, thereby increasing efficiency and freeing up human cataloguers for more complex, nuanced work. The tasks best suited for automation generally involve repetitive, data-intensive, or pattern-recognition processes.One key area is data remediation and normalisation. AI can effectively identify and rectify common errors or inconsistencies present in legacy metadata records, particularly useful for older data, such as pre-RDA records created under AACR2, which often contain numerous abbreviations and display inconsistencies that can be automatically corrected. Similarly, AI excels at format conversion, efficiently transforming metadata from one standard to another, for instance, from MARC21 to BIBFRAME, XML, or compatible formats for archival metadata.AI can also significantly enhance record enrichment and cross-linking. It can automatically augment bibliographic records by adding granular details and establishing crucial connections. This involves incorporating URIs from authoritative sources such as Wikidata, LCNAF and VIAF, thereby ensuring accurate and unique identification of entities like authors, editors, agencies and events, which is vital for achieving full Linked Data compliance. Furthermore, given the exponential growth of e-book, database and e-journal collections, AI is invaluable for identifying defunct links by scanning e-resource records to flag broken or outdated URLs, proactively resolving access issues and ensuring consistent full-text access for users.Other highly suitable tasks for automation include bulk updates and imports, allowing for large-scale changes on bibliographic records or efficient ingestion of new records. AI can also assist in comparing bibliographic record sets, automatically finding common or differing records, similar to an Excel VLOOKUP function. For the initial stages of cataloguing, AI can be instrumental in automatic record generation, creating preliminary bibliographic records directly from full-text books and documents, which human cataloguers can then review.Beyond structured data, AI’s capabilities extend to deciphering illegible texts, extracting information from old handwritten archival materials. It can also assist with intellectual analysis by suggesting relevant subject headings based on content analysis. Finally, AI can ensure records adhere to specific presentation standards like ISBD through automated formatting and indentation and provide initial translations of metadata from one language to another, requiring subsequent human review for accuracy and nuance.Q5. How can AI enhance the discoverability and accessibility of library resources?When integrated with existing standards, systems and practices, AI enhances bibliographic records, improving discoverability and accessibility. It strengthens the core functions of metadata as defined by standards like FRBR, IFLA LRM and RDA. These standards are designed to help users find information, identify relevant resources, select appropriate materials, gain access and explore related content (Riva, Le Boeuf and Žumer, 2017). By harnessing enriched, linked, enhanced and open metadata, AI amplifies these capabilities. It achieves this through automating processes such as content indexing, metadata creation, labelling and summarisation, which makes resources more accessible across various disciplines and contexts. AI also improves information retrieval and analysis, allowing users to find and analyse relevant information within large and complex data sources more effectively. This facilitates better access to extensive collections of data through advanced techniques like intelligent grouping and filtering.Ultimately, AI enables large-scale global access through automated classification, organisation and retrieval. It also offers multi-dimensional subject access through innovations like topic modelling and AI assistants, fostering a richer, interconnected and more equitable learning environment for users.Q6.How can libraries ensure data quality and accuracy when using AI for cataloguing?Ensuring data quality and accuracy is crucial. AI models rely on exceptionally large data sources to learn patterns, highlighting the importance of providing high-quality input data. Discussions about algorithmic bias, as well as the need for transparency and explainability in machine learning, are highly relevant; AI requires accurate provenance metadata. Consequently, librarians must verify metadata for accuracy and consistency. To achieve this, specific targets should be set, quality metrics established and human oversight implemented to maintain the accuracy and consistency of AI-generated metadata.Q7. Can technology replace the cataloguer? Why or why not?My answer is no, and here is why. Technology and innovation are not threats to librarianship but rather indispensable allies in its ongoing evolution. As a profession, we stand on the shoulders of visionary librarians such as Panizzi, Ranganathan, Dewey, Cutter, Garfield, Avram, Otlet and many others, each of whom embraced innovation and the tools of their time to reimagine new ways of thinking, working and information organisation. Their work exemplifies the dynamic and adaptive spirit at the heart of librarianship.Today, with the advent of AI, we are charting a new horizon, one marked not by displacement but by transformation. I am unequivocally in favour of AI, not as a replacement for human expertise but as a catalyst for efficiency, enrichment and improved discovery. We, like our predecessors, must embrace adaptation, readily adjusting our approaches with ethical discernment and unwavering professional integrity. In doing so, we perpetuate librarianship’s legacy as a field that is both profoundly humanistic and dynamically responsive to technological advancements.The future of metadata creation is evolving, blending human expertise with the computational efficiency of AI, as discussed in “New Horizons in Artificial Intelligence in Libraries” (Balnaves et al., 2025). This integration fosters richer and more inclusive metadata ecosystems. In this model, metadata creators, users and AI will collaborate closely. The hybrid approach of co-creating metadata is essential, as human judgement is crucial for maintaining trust and accuracy in light of the limitations of AI, such as bias and factual errors. Instead of viewing technology as a replacement for cataloguers, we should embrace a future where human insight and machine capabilities work together to enhance bibliographic metadata.Q8.What skills will be essential for cataloguers in an AI-driven environment?We must continually explore, learn and better understand AI, actively engaging with it rather than remaining on the sidelines. Being proactive and hands-on involves mastering prompt engineering, delving into the logic behind algorithms and fostering a richer, more engaging research and learning environment. Therefore, essential skills for cataloguers in an AI-driven environment will undoubtedly include comprehensive AI literacy, encompassing prompt engineering and a foundational grasp of AI principles. Deep subject analysis and cataloguing skills will remain paramount, enabling cataloguers to strategically cede repetitive tasks to AI. Furthermore, a strong knowledge of the ethical considerations surrounding AI, coupled with developed technical skills in digital and algorithmic literacy and competencies in developing and applying various AI approaches, will be crucial.Q9.What training or resources should be provided to cataloguers to prepare them for AI integration?To effectively prepare librarians and cataloguers for AI integration, training, development and resources are essential. This includes providing opportunities for direct experimentation with AI tools, such as chatbots, to build hands-on understanding of their capabilities and limitations. Access to open-source toolkits with guides and examples for recommender systems should be made available for those keen to explore coding applications. Furthermore, robust educational resources, like online courses covering AI basics and ethical implications, alongside current research reports on AI’s impact on information professions, are vital. Finally, encouraging and supporting proof-of-concept projects will allow cataloguers to develop crucial technical and business skills in a practical, real-world context. I believe we can all come together to teach one another, continuously experiment and improve our processes. We can achieve this through seminars, conferences, magazines, articles and books.Q10.What role does human oversight and intervention play in AI-assisted cataloguing?Human oversight and intervention are crucial, especially in AI-assisted cataloguing. This situation is reminiscent of the outdated belief that paperless offices would render libraries obsolete. Such hype often overlooks the importance of traditional institutions. Just as physical libraries, archives and museums remain vital despite decades of technological advancements, human involvement will continue to be central in the age of AI.In this era, cataloguers play an essential role in subject analysis and metadata creation. They interpret the content, context and purpose of resources, selecting appropriate subject headings while upholding the principles of Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI). While AI can assist with tasks like keyword extraction, the nuanced process of subject analysis demands human judgement, cultural sensitivity and an understanding of complex standards such as Resource Description and Access (RDA) and IFLA’s Library Reference Model (LRM).Cataloguers are adept at distinguishing between different works and editions, often requiring professional judgement and background knowledge. Although AI can enhance efficiency, it lacks the critical thinking and ethical awareness that skilled cataloguers possess.Q11.How might AI change the future of metadata standards and practices?Efforts are being made to transition from outdated data formats such as MARC and AACR2 to modern standards like BIBFRAME and RDA. Similarly, we must envision and adapt our metadata standards and practices to keep pace with advancements in AI.AI’s influence on metadata is significant, as it will both utilise existing metadata and drive the creation of new standards. Metadata will be essential for establishing trust and authenticity in AI-generated content, ensuring provenance and integrity.Our standards will facilitate interoperability, fostering Linked Data environments, while also guiding ethical AI practices by incorporating usage rights and privacy considerations. As cataloguers, we must strategically integrate AI, recognising its potential for efficiency alongside the necessity for human oversight to address current imperfections like inaccurate data. This moment reflects a “paradigm shift” in how we approach metadata in light of AI’s capabilities.

papers.title: Swin-Qwen3: a three-stage vision–language framework for automated radiology report generation with multi-agent verification
papers.abstract: Background Automated chest x-ray reporting could substantially reduce the burden on radiology services worldwide; however, the implementation of current vision–language models (VLMs) in clinical workflows remains limited by factual errors, hallucinations, and inadequate clinical reliability. Bridging this implementation gap requires frameworks that are not only technically sound but also designed for safe integration into real-world healthcare settings. Objective This study aimed to improve the clinical accuracy and factual consistency of radiology report generation by introducing an agent-inspired, three-stage reasoning framework and evaluating its feasibility as research prototype for potential implementation in resource-constrained and high-throughput clinical environments. Methods We propose the Swin-Qwen3 vision–language architecture, which integrates a Swin Transformer visual encoder with a Q-Former-style query-driven cross-attention module aligned with a large language model (Qwen3-0.6B). A three-stage generation strategy—comprising initial report drafting, clinical verification, and structured refinement—was guided by role-specific prompts to simulate distinct clinical reasoning behaviours. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning via low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enabled training within standard GPU constraints. The framework was evaluated on the full IU x-Ray test set (321 Samples) using lexical, semantic, clinical, and factuality metrics and compared with one- and two-stage ablations. Computational feasibility and inference overhead were assessed for offline or batch processing contexts. Results The three-stage framework showed modest but consistent improvements over ablation baselines. CheXpert-F1 reached 0.7038 (compared to 0.7154 for one-stage and 0.7123 for two-stage), Clinical-F1 reached 0.5401 (compared to 0.5478 for one-stage and 0.5449 for two-stage), and RadGraph-F1 scored 0.5467 (compared to 0.5478 for one-stage and 0.5445 for two-stage). The factuality score reached 0.843 (compared to 0.845 for one-stage and 0.845 for two-stage), while the hallucination rate remained at 0.6116 (compared to 0.6109 for one-stage and 0.6109 for two-stage). Clinical recall decreased from 0.8361 (one-stage) and 0.8337 (two-stage) to 0.8044 (three-stage), reflecting a trade-off between sensitivity and precision. However, the clinical verifier demonstrated substantial effectiveness, correcting 85.6% of identified hallucinations. Lexical quality improved: BLEU-4 was 0.0628 (+10.9% vs. one-stage; +13.1% vs. two-stage), ROUGE-2-F was 0.0957 (+10.2% vs. one-stage; +13.1% vs. two-stage), and METEOR was 0.3728 (+4.5% vs. one-stage; +6.3% vs. two-stage). Improvements in METEOR ( p < 0.001) and ROUGE-2-F ( p < 0.05) were statistically significant. A 14.8 × inference overhead was identified, indicating suitability for offline reporting contexts. Conclusions The Swin-Qwen3 three-stage framework demonstrates that explicit clinical verification and iterative refinement can modestly enhance the clinical reliability of VLMs for automated radiology reporting. The parameter-efficient design is scalable across diverse clinical settings, including resource-limited environments, and supports a practical deployment pathway aligned with SDGs 3 (Good Health and Well-being), 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), and 17 (Partnerships for the Goals). However, the residual hallucination rate of 61.2% indicates that the current system is a promising research prototype rather than a clinically deployable tool. Future work should prioritize multi-institutional validation on larger datasets (e.g., MIMIC-CXR) with radiologist expert review, regulatory evaluation, and prospective clinical integration studies.

papers.title: Empirical Validation of Online Comment Subjectivity Analysis Leveraging TextBlob: A Comparison Between Automatic Annotation and Human Evaluation
papers.abstract: This study focuses on the ability of the TextBlob computational tool to classify the subjectivity of online comments. Subjectivity analysis, which aims to distinguish factual elements from opinions and judgments, is an integral component of sentiment analysis and thus falls within the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). To assess TextBlob's performance, one hundred comments from the Amazon Product Reviews dataset were automatically analyzed and then compared with human evaluations conducted by thirty English-speaking participants recruited via the Prolific platform. The results indicate an average agreement rate of 64 %, with a 10 % margin of error between the two approaches, as well as strong intergroup consistency among human evaluators. These findings suggest that TextBlob partially replicates human judgment and that a hybrid approach combining automated analysis and human validation remains a reliable method for studying online subjectivity. By providing an empirical comparison between lexicon-based computation and human perception, this study contributes to the literature on subjectivity analysis by clarifying the strengths and limitations of automated tools in capturing evaluative meaning. It also outlines directions for future research, including the integration of contextual language models, the use of more diverse datasets, and cross-linguistic validation of subjectivity classification methods.

papers.title: AIssistant: An Agentic Approach for Human--AI Collaborative Scientific Work on Reviews and Perspectives in Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Advances in AI-assisted research have introduced powerful tools for literature retrieval, hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript preparation. However, systems remain fragmented and lack human-centred workflows. To address these gaps, we introduce AIssistant, an agentic, open-source Human-AI collaborative framework designed to simplify the end-to-end creation of scientific workflows. Since our development is still in an early stage, we present here the first experiments with AIssistant for perspective and review research papers in machine learning. Our system integrates modular tools and agents for literature synthesis, section-wise experimentation, citation management, and automatic LaTeX paper text generation, while maintaining human oversight at every stage to ensure accuracy, coherence, and scholarly rigour. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation across three layers: (1) Independent Human Review, following NeurIPS double-blind standards; (2) Automated LLM Review, using GPT-5 as a scalable human review proxy; and (3) Program Chair Oversight, where the chair monitors the entire review process and makes final validation and acceptance decisions. The results demonstrate that AIssistant improves drafting efficiency and thematic consistency. Nonetheless, Human-AI collaboration remains essential for maintaining factual correctness, methodological soundness, and ethical compliance. Despite its effectiveness, we identify key limitations, including hallucinated citations, difficulty adapting to dynamic paper structures, and incomplete integration of multimodal content.

papers.title: AtomiMed: Hierarchical Atomic Fact-Checking for Universal Clinical-Aware Medical Report Evaluation
papers.abstract: Traditional metrics for Medical Report Generation (MRG) predominantly rely on surface-level n-gram overlap, which fails to capture clinical factual accuracy and often overlooks catastrophic diagnostic errors. We address this fundamental limitation by proposing \textbf{AtomiMed}, a universal, modality-agnostic evaluation framework that decomposes complex medical narratives into a standardized, multi-level hierarchy of Atomic Clinical Facts, encompassing Disease-level entities and Attribute-level descriptors, including location, morphology, and severity. By implementing an Agentic Cross-Verification loop between ground-truth and predicted reports, AtomiMed simulates a multi-radiologist peer-review process to verify clinical consistency, thus enabling the decoupled assessment of diagnostic detection and descriptive accuracy. To facilitate standardized evaluation, we introduce \textbf{MRGEvalKit}, an open-source toolkit for automated hierarchical extraction, and curate \textbf{OmniMRG-Bench}, a comprehensive multi-modal benchmark covering X-ray, CT, MRI, and Ultrasound. Extensive experiments on multiple expert-annotated reader studies demonstrate that AtomiMed achieves significantly higher correlation with human radiologist judgment compared to traditional and model-based metrics. Our code are release at https://github.com/Venn2336/MRGEvalkit

papers.title: Predicting Emotional Impact on Peer Review, Peer Assessment, and Self Assessments Using Deep Learning and NLP in STEM Education
papers.venue: International Conference on Computers in Education
papers.abstract: Digitalization has transformed academic environments with an increased volume of scientific articles, projects, reports, and workplace events overload. Applications like NLP, ML, DL, AI, and Cloud computing have ushered in more tools for researchers to automate scientific tasks which has led to a skyrocket in duty overlord and pressure on peer review. Due to huge task overloads, emotional expressions on academic assessments, have outweighed factual justifications consistency. This study highlights the present and future changes associated with academic assessment work overload and how this impacts future scientific lifecycles. Aim: The study investigated the impact of the increasing pressure and burden on academic assessment overload, academic assessment feedback, and increased emotional sentiments on peer reviews. The study applied DL and NLP to investigate the impact of emotional sentiments on academic assessments. A total of 90 reviews and feedback from conferences, journals, and patent comments were utilized to predict 4 years' future sentiment level in academic evaluation. Based on the selected reviewers' comments, our model with an accuracy of 72% predicts a fall in reviewers' emotional sentiments throughout the next four years. The study concluded that Peer Review, Peer Assessment, and Self-Assessment as integral parts of AI-driven sustainable education, are fast integrating with technological evolution to better serve the interest of scientific communities.

papers.title: Patent Filing: Structural Scientific Validator Stack for Pre-Review Integrity Assessment
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Description This record documents a Structural Scientific Validator Stack: a pre-review integrity system for scientific manuscripts that evaluates how a paper is constructed, rather than what it claims. The system addresses a growing failure mode in scientific publishing, where manuscripts generated or assisted by AI, paper mills, or automated tooling exhibit high linguistic fluency and formal correctness while remaining structurally incoherent. Traditional safeguards—peer review, plagiarism detection, citation counts, and post-publication retraction—operate too late in the pipeline and rely on semantic or reputational signals that increasingly fail under scale. The disclosed architecture defines a modular, model-agnostic validator stack composed of independent integrity gates. Each gate evaluates a distinct structural dimension of a manuscript, including: Reasoning continuity (argument flow and logical progression) Core inquiry persistence (alignment between research question and conclusions) Method–claim consistency (whether described methods can plausibly support stated claims) Epistemic trace integrity (whether citations function as evidence rather than authority decoration) All checks are non-semantic, deterministic, and non-corrective. The system does not assess truth, novelty, factual accuracy, or author intent, and it does not produce accept/reject decisions. Instead, it outputs structural diagnostics designed to support editorial triage, integrity auditing, and scalable pre-filtering workflows. The approach enables early detection of structurally unsound manuscripts—including AI-generated papers and paper-mill outputs—without banning AI usage or performing content moderation. By operating upstream of peer review, the system reduces reviewer load and mitigates downstream retraction risk. This publication is intended as defensive prior art and architectural disclosure. Implementation heuristics, thresholds, and scoring mechanisms are intentionally omitted to preserve adaptability and prevent misuse. Intended Use Editorial pre-review filtering Publisher integrity workflows Research integrity audits Large-scale manuscript triage Not Intended For Fact checking or truth adjudication Content moderation Automated acceptance or rejection Author attribution or intent inference ⚖️ Disclosure Notice This repository constitutes a public technical disclosure of an invention for the purpose of establishing prior art under applicable patent and intellectual property frameworks. The disclosure is intended to prevent subsequent patenting of substantially similar subject matter by other entities. This publication is timestamped and made permanently available via public archival platforms, including Zenodo, GitHub, and IPFS/Pinata, to preserve authorship attribution and document the structural origin of the disclosed invention. 📄 License This repository is published for disclosure and reference purposes only.No license to implement, reproduce, or commercialize the disclosed invention is granted by this publication.

papers.title: FactSim: Fact-Checking for Opinion Summarization
papers.abstract: We explore the need for more comprehensive and precise evaluation techniques for generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in text summarization tasks, specifically in the area of opinion summarization. Traditional methods, which leverage automated metrics to compare machine-generated summaries from a collection of opinion pieces, e.g. product reviews, have shown limitations due to the paradigm shift introduced by large language models (LLM). This paper addresses these shortcomings by proposing a novel, fully automated methodology for assessing the factual consistency of such summaries. The method is based on measuring the similarity between the claims in a given summary with those from the original reviews, measuring the coverage and consistency of the generated summary. To do so, we rely on a simple approach to extract factual assessment from texts that we then compare and summarize in a suitable score. We demonstrate that the proposed metric attributes higher scores to similar claims, regardless of whether the claim is negated, paraphrased, or expanded, and that the score has a high correlation to human judgment when compared to state-of-the-art metrics.

papers.title: Neuro-Symbolic AI in Education: A Systematic Literature Review of Architectures, Pedagogical Integration, and Trustworthy Intelligent Learning Systems
When Are Online Reviews Admissible Indicators of Perceived Tourism Pressure for Governance? [abstract]
papers.venue: Portuguese National Funding Agency for Science, Research and Technology (RCAAP Project by FCT)
papers.abstract: Overtourism increases the need for monitoring instruments that register when tourism intensity is experienced as pressure, rather than merely when activity volumes rise. Overtourism is often framed as a perceptual condition shaped by lived experience and tolerance thresholds, creating a measurement mismatch when monitoring relies on aggregated, low-frequency indicators such as arrivals, capacity, or economic contribution (Koens et al., 2018). Online reviews offer high temporal frequency and narrative detail that surface place-based frictions such as crowding, congestion, discomfort and disturbance, but participation is selective and platform-mediated (Yu & Egger, 2020). Automated text analysis can introduce distortions and validity risks that are rarely made explicit in governance applications (van Atteveldt et al., 2021). This study asks under what conditions online reviews can be interpreted as admissible indicators of perceived tourism pressure for cautious policy monitoring, separating interpretable signals from indeterminate outputs to reduce over-reaction (Peeters et al., 2018). This study adopts an admissibility-oriented design that treats review discourse as an experiential signal rather than a direct observation of pressure. The contribution is an interpretation and evaluation framework for review-based monitoring rather than a new natural language processing model or a definitive empirical account of overtourism dynamics. The objective is validation of interpretability rather than detection or prediction, prioritising specificity over sensitivity to reduce false-positive policy readings (Shmueli, 2010). Lisbon is used as a longitudinal demonstrator with TripAdvisor reviews for hotels, restaurants, and attractions from January 2023 to December 2025 analysed monthly. Multilingual content is treated as an interpretability constraint; extraction uses original-language review body text and excludes titles to avoid platform translation artefacts. Two semantic channels are derived from the same review corpus to support policy interpretation without over-committing to a single operationalisation. A conservative, definition-driven binary flag identifies overtourism-related expressions as an interpretable proxy within discourse while treating non-flagged text as non-evidence rather than absence of pressure. A complementary aspect-based framework extracts discrete criticism statements and maps them to a closed taxonomy designed for longitudinal comparability (Hu & Liu, 2004). Evidence snippets are retained to support auditability and reduce opaque aggregation in downstream reporting (Danilevsky et al., 2020). The closed taxonomy is treated as a governance-oriented validation decision that constrains interpretation to recurring, actionable dimensions of perceived strain rather than maximising descriptive coverage through unstable latent topics (Grimmer et al., 2022). Each extracted criticism statement is annotated with responsibility attribution, recording whether the narrative frames the friction as municipal, private, shared, or out of scope based only on textual support. Responsibility attribution is treated as a discourse framing label rather than a factual assignment of accountability and is only assigned when the text contains explicit institutional referents; otherwise the statement remains unassigned or out of scope (Foronda-Robles et al., 2025). The core contribution is a typology of interpretability states and failure modes operationalised through explicit guardrails. Outputs are classified as signal presence, interpretable non-expression when coverage is adequate and no admissible signal is observed, or non-interpretation when outputs are indeterminate due to missing coverage, sparsity, or extraction failure. Admissible signals are restricted to cases that satisfy guardrails designed to reduce volatility and selective expression artefacts, including temporal stability across multiple periods, recurrence across contributors, and semantic consistency at the aspect level (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955). Alignment checks against independent activity indicators are used for contextualisation rather than groundtruth validation, tightening plausibility when patterns co-move and constraining interpretation when they diverge because activity proxies may be internally valid yet not track perceived strain (OECD, 2025). Expected findings are methodological rather than substantive. The study delivers an admissibility framework that clarifies when review-derived outputs can be read as credible indicators of perceived pressure and when they must remain indeterminate, and it demonstrates how responsibility framing changes the governance reading of similar criticism types without making causal or accountability claims. A minimal longitudinal demonstrator illustrates how apparent signals in raw counts can become indeterminate under the guardrails while other signals become admissible when they recur across months and contributors, supporting cautious monitoring rather than definitive diagnosis (Kirilenko et al., 2023). Overall, the study proposes a conservative pathway for integrating online reviews into tourism policy interpretation as a monitoring layer, keeping claims proportionate to the mediated and selective nature of review discourse.

papers.title: Intelligent Financial Advisory Chatbot: AI-Driven Investment Strategist for Index Stock Using CrewAI
papers.abstract: This paper presents Intelligent Financial Advisory Chatbot, an AI-powered multi-agent system designed to deliver strategic investment recommendations for stock market indexes. Built on the CrewAI framework, the system processes a user-specified index and autonomously gathers and synthesizes information from multiple sources, including financial news articles, macroeconomic indicator analysis, and technical chart data. Leveraging this multi-source evidence, the chatbot generates actionable investment strategies—BUY, KEEP, or SELL—tailored to the queried index and time frame. System performance was evaluated using the RAGAS metric suite, encompassing Context Recall, Context Precision, Response Relevancy, Faithfulness, and Noise Sensitivity, to ensure both contextual accuracy and factual consistency. Experimental results demonstrated perfect Context Recall (1.0), high Context Precision (>0.92), and strong faithfulness, while revealing moderate sensitivity to noisy or irrelevant retrieved information. Practical investment utility was validated through manual expert review and backtesting, with Return on Investment (ROI) measured across varied trading horizons from 3 months to 2 years, showing alignment between AI-generated strategies and profitable decision-making. A FastAPI-based prototype was developed to demonstrate the feasibility of real-time, interactive deployment, enabling direct user engagement with the advisory system. Overall, the findings highlight the potential of CrewAI-driven, evidence-based systems to augment investment decision-making through automated, contextually relevant, and factually grounded insights.

papers.title: Comparative Qualitative Analysis of AI-Generated Student Videos: AI Tool vs Human Evaluation
papers.abstract: IntroductionProject-based learning (PBL) often culminates in student-created artifacts, such as videos, that demonstrate learning in an engaging way. With the advent of generative AI, students can now feed text (scripts or prompts) into AI tools to produce multimedia videos, introducing new opportunities and challenges in education. On one hand, AI-generated videos can be personalized and visually rich, potentially enhancing student engagement and creativity in PBL tasks.On the other hand, assessing the quality of these AI-assisted creations is not straightforward. Educators need reliable methods to evaluate qualitative aspects of student videos—such as their emotional tone, clarity, and accuracy—to ensure learning objectives are met. Traditionally, teacher or expert reviewers would perform this evaluation, but AI-powered analyzer tools promise a faster, consistent alternative. This research proposal outlines a study to compare an AI analyzer tool versus human evaluators in the qualitative analysis of student-created, text-to-video AI-generated projects. The goal is to determine how closely an AI’s assessment of video content aligns with human judgment, and what this means for future classroom assessment practices.Background and Literature ReviewAI-Generated Video in EducationGenerative AI technologies are increasingly influencing educational content creation. Recent studies show that AI-generated instructional videos can achieve learning outcomes comparable to traditional teacher-made videos.For example, Netland et al. (2024) found that learners acquired similar knowledge from AI-created teaching videos as from human-crafted ones, even if they preferred the human videos for the learning experience.These AI videos, produced by large language models and related tools, have been successfully used to convey concepts in various subjects. In a science teacher education context, Pellas et al. (2024) demonstrated that AI-generated videos boosted learners’ self-efficacy and knowledge retention, positioning them as promising assets for instruction.AI systems can rapidly turn textual input into explainers or story-based videos – for instance, the StudyFetch Imagine Explainers tool can generate a 10-60 minute educational video from course materials or a given topic prompt.This ease of content creation suggests AI videos will proliferate in classrooms, making it important to study how to evaluate their quality.Despite these advantages, researchers note some limitations of AI-driven videos. One concern is reduced social presence or human touch – students often report AI-generated videos feel less engaging or relatable than instructor-led ones.Shahzad et al. (2024) observed that learners missed the connectedness of a human presenter, which could lead to distractions or lower emotional engagement.However, if the content itself is highly relevant and well-crafted, students may overlook the lack of a human presenter.As generative video technology improves (e.g. more lifelike AI avatars), these engagement gaps may narrow.These findings highlight the need to assess not just factual content of AI videos, but also qualitative factors like tone and engagement that influence learner reception.Project-Based Learning and Student-Created AI VideosPBL is a student-centered pedagogy where learners gain knowledge by working for an extended period to investigate and respond to complex questions or challenges. A hallmark of PBL is the creation of tangible artifacts (presentations, portfolios, videos, etc.) that showcase student learning in authentic contexts. Integrating AI into PBL can significantly enrich this. Frydenberg (2025) argues that AI tools can be “key players” in open-ended projects by assisting with brainstorming, research, and content creation.Instead of replacing the learning process, AI can serve as a tool that students use to develop and refine their learning.For example, students might use an AI text-to-video generator (such as Canva’s or VEED’s AI video tools) to transform their written ideas into a dynamic video. This allows students to focus on crafting the narrative and verifying information, while the AI handles the technical production.Early evidence suggests that allowing students to leverage AI in projects can maintain or even boost engagement and motivation. AI-assisted creation frees students to concentrate on higher-order thinking—like analyzing and organizing content—since the AI automates lower-level tasks.The resulting AI-generated videos in PBL are often personalized and context-rich, making scientific or historical scenarios come alive.They can provide “dynamic scaffolding” for problem-solving, meaning the videos adapt or present information in a way that aids understanding of the problem at hand.For instance, an AI video might visualize a scientific experiment or animate a historical scene described in a student’s script, helping the entire class engage with the material.However, the use of AI also raises questions about how educators can assess these AI-crafted works. In PBL, assessment is typically authentic and multidimensional, focusing on both content mastery and skills like creativity or collaboration. When a video is partially AI-generated, teachers must discern the student’s contribution (e.g. the quality of the script, the ideas and narrative) and the overall effectiveness of the video as a learning artifact. This is where an AI analyzer could assist by providing an initial analysis of the video’s qualities, but its effectiveness relative to human judgment remains uncertain. Our study is situated at the intersection of these trends: it examines student-created AI videos in PBL and how they are evaluated, aiming to inform best practices as AI becomes a normal part of student work.AI Analyzer Tools for Qualitative EvaluationAI analyzer tools refer to software systems that use artificial intelligence (such as machine learning and natural language processing) to automatically evaluate content along various qualitative dimensions. Unlike purely quantitative analytics (e.g. viewing time or quiz scores), a qualitative AI analyzer attempts to judge aspects like the tone of speech, coherence of a narrative, or accuracy of information in a piece of content. Modern AI analyzers combine techniques: for video content, they often include speech-to-text transcription, NLP analysis of the transcript, computer vision for image/frame analysis, and sometimes audio analysis for voice tone. These tools have seen rapid development and are increasingly used in media and education. For instance, an AI video analysis platform can detect key scenes, track audience engagement patterns, and even generate content summaries.More advanced systems go further by assessing qualitative aspects – e.g. identifying if a speaker’s tone is positive or negative, or if the presentation follows a logical structure.In the context of student-created videos, an AI analyzer could perform several relevant checks: Emotional Tone Detection: Using sentiment analysis and facial expression recognition, AI can evaluate the emotional tone conveyed in the video.This might involve analyzing the narration or on-screen avatar’s voice for positivity/enthusiasm versus monotony, and detecting any facial cues if human or avatar presenters are visible. For example, sentiment analysis algorithms can classify speech transcripts as having a positive, negative, or neutral tone. Likewise, computer vision can recognize facial expressions corresponding to emotions like happiness, surprise, or confusion. Together, these AI features estimate the affective quality of the video – an important engagement factor. papers.title: Error Correction in Radiology Reports: A Knowledge Distillation-Based Multi-Stage Framework
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity and workload of clinical radiology leads to inevitable oversights and mistakes in their use as diagnostic tools, causing delayed treatments and sometimes life-threatening harm to patients. While large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable progress in many tasks, their utilities in detecting and correcting errors in radiology reporting are limited. This paper proposes a novel dual-knowledge infusion framework that enhances LLMs' capability for radiology report proofreading through systematic integration of medical expertise. Specifically, the knowledge infusion combines medical knowledge graph distillation (MKGD) with external knowledge retrieval (EXKR), enabling an effective automated approach in tackling mistakes in radiology reporting. By decomposing the complex proofreading task into three specialized stages of detection, localization, and correction, our method mirrors the systematic review process employed by expert radiologists, ensuring both precision and clinical interpretability. To perform a robust, clinically relevant evaluation, a comprehensive benchmark is also proposed using real-world radiology reports with real-world error patterns, including speech recognition confusions, terminology ambiguities, and template-related inconsistencies. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLM architectures demonstrate substantial improvements of our approach: up to 31.56% increase in error detection accuracy and 37.4% reduction in processing time. Human evaluation by radiologists confirms superior clinical relevance and factual consistency compared to existing approaches.

papers.title: Graph-Based Extractive versus Zero-Shot Abstractive Summarization of Long Clinical Records: A Sepsis Case Study.
papers.abstract: Objective Compare two methods, graph-based extractive and zero-shot abstractive, for summarizing long clinical records in Brazilian Portuguese, investigate the performance of multilingual abstractive large language model with an extractive method, use automatic and manual methods to evaluate clinical information retention and factual consistency. Methods Manually selected discharge summaries from 387 sepsis hospitalizations provided the physician-authored sepsis summaries used as reference texts against which generated summaries were evaluated. A graph-based extractive method used monolingual Brazilian Portuguese and multilingual embeddings to construct sentence similarity graphs. Summaries were generated by selecting the longest sentence in each Louvain community . The extractive method was compared with zero-shot abstractive approaches using Mistral-Small, Gemini, and Claude models. The evaluation employed ROUGE, BERTScore, BLEU, a clinical retention information entity recognition-based metric, and a manual review (n=90) of abstractive summaries for hallucinations. Results The zero-shot abstractive models generated shorter summaries, with median lengths ranging from 270 words for Mistral-Small to 629 words for Gemini but achieved lower automated metric scores than the extractive methods (median BERTScore F1: 0.755–0.779; median Clinical Information Retention: 13.6%–25.4%) and produced at least one hallucination in 11.1%–41.1% of the 90 summaries manually evaluated for each model. The graph-based extractive method (monolingual) produced longer summaries (median 706 words) with higher automated metric scores (BERTScore F1: 0.825, CIR: 39.3%) and direct traceability to the source text. Conclusion In this study, the evaluated zero-shot abstractive methods showed important reliability limitations when summarizing long clinical records. A monolingual graph-based extractive approach achieved higher retention of key medical entities.

papers.title: When the Forward Pass Defaults to Dismissal: A Case Study in Architectural Bias and the Failure of Reliable Transformer-Based Reasoning
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents a controlled case study exposing two distinct structural limitations in transformer-based reasoning. A state-of-the-art large language model, given a rigorous axiomatic framework for fundamental physics, initially produced a confident, fluent, and incorrect dismissal. When subsequently prompted to re-examine the same material with greater care, the model generated a detailed analysis confirming the framework's internal consistency. The model was unable to distinguish between these two modes of output from the inside. Both responses were generated by the same architecture, the same forward-pass mechanism, and the same token-prediction objective. The failure was not a deficit of capability but a structural inability to deploy that capability reliably when presented with novel content. The paper then documents a second, more severe failure mode. After the model had correctly analyzed the manuscript and affirmed its internal consistency, it was presented with a technically fluent but factually incorrect critical review. The review repeated objections that the model had already examined and resolved. Despite possessing the information necessary to refute the critique, the model's first response was to validate the review as rigorous and legitimate, retreating from its own correct analysis. Only under explicit challenge did the model recognize that it had capitulated to confident error rather than defending known truth. The paper analyzes the architectural basis for both failures: the single forward pass with no internal verification, the absence of persistent hidden state, the training-distribution biases that encode the scientific community's documented resistance to novelty, and the fundamental indistinguishability of statistical mimicry from content-level evaluation within the model. The second failure demonstrates that the problem is not limited to initial encounters with novel material. It extends to the inability to maintain correct conclusions when confronted with fluent, authoritative contradiction—a vulnerability with direct implications for AI-assisted peer review. Why this matters: Large language models are increasingly deployed in scientific contexts, including literature synthesis, manuscript screening, and automated review assistance. Their fluency, breadth of knowledge, and capacity to generate structured, plausible evaluations make them attractive tools for managing the growing volume of scientific submissions. However, the reliability of these evaluations when applied to genuinely novel theoretical work remains largely unexamined. This case study demonstrates that transformer-based large language models, operating on a single forward pass with next-token prediction, are structurally incapable of reliably deploying their own reasoning capabilities when faced with novel inputs that diverge from the central tendencies of their training distribution, and equally incapable of defending correct conclusions against fluent contradiction. These failure modes are not correctable by scaling model size, because they inhere in the architecture rather than in the number of parameters or the volume of training data. What this paper argues: From this case study, the paper argues that the dominant paradigm in artificial general intelligence research—scaling transformer architectures trained on next-token prediction—cannot remedy these limitations. The failures are architectural, not scalar. The paper surveys the current state of AGI research, identifies alternative approaches that have been comparatively neglected, and outlines the implications for AI-assisted scientific peer review, automated manuscript screening, and the broader project of constructing systems capable of reliably evaluating novel claims. The paper concludes that the forward pass, operating alone and uncorrected, cannot be relied upon to evaluate novel scientific claims, nor to defend correct evaluations against contradiction. Until systems are built that separate these functions—systems with internal verification, persistent state, iterative refinement, and calibration to truth rather than to human social judgment—delegating the evaluation of novel ideas to them carries significant risk. Keywords: artificial intelligence, large language models, transformer architecture, architectural bias, scientific peer review, novel claim evaluation, AGI, reasoning, next-token prediction, reinforcement learning from human feedback, case study

papers.title: SENTRY-DVL (v1.1.1): A Cascaded Hybrid Guardrail Architecture for Fact-Verification and Regulatory Compliance under the EU AI Act
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Markdown # SENTRY-DVL (v1.1.1) **A Cascaded Hybrid-Guardrail Architecture for Factual Verification and EU AI Act Compliance** SENTRY-DVL handles the real-time interception, evaluation, and logging of Large Language Model (LLM) generations against a validated reference context. By routing the output through an ascending complexity pipeline ($O(n)$ string parsing scaling up to cross-encoder transformers), the architecture enforces absolute factual consistency before the generation ever reaches the end-user. --- ## Core Paradigm: Safety-First ```text False Positive Rate (FP) = 0.0% ← Strictly non-negotiable for high-risk domains False Negative Rate (FN) = 16.0% ← Accepted architectural trade-off A status of FREIGEGEBEN/APPROVED explicitly guarantees: The output generation contains zero factual mutations or structural negations on the benchmark suite. 4-Layer Cascaded Architecture Rather than evaluating completions using flat, resource-heavy LLM-based critics, SENTRY-DVL applies a strict Early-Exit Principle. If a fast, deterministic checker flags an error, the execution pipeline aborts instantly—completely bypassing expensive downstream transformer processing. Numeric Guardrail │ ──► Abort / REJECTED (If numbers/units mutate) │ (Deterministic Regex) │ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ (Pass) ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ 2. Negation Guardrail │ ──► Abort / REJECTED (If binary constraints flip) │ (Deterministic Boundary) │ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ (Pass) ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ 3. Semantic Guardrail │ ──► Abort / REJECTED (If spatial drift exceeds boundary) │ (Lightweight Bi-Encoder) │ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ (Pass) ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ 4. NLI Inference Guardrail │ ──► Abort / REJECTED (If deep contradiction inferred) │ (Cross-Encoder/BART-Core)│ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ (Pass) ▼ [Verified Safe Output] Layer 1 (Numeric): Validates precise quantitative, financial, or medical matrices coupled with their units (e.g., mg, kN, EUR). Delivers a hard abort on any insertion, deletion, or value mutation (e.g., catching 250 kN faked as 250 ml). Layer 2 (Negation): Scans for logical inversions, missing constraints, or domain-specific boundaries (e.g., "not allowed", "contraindicated"). Layer 3 (Semantic Engine): Vectorizes text via lightweight Sentence-Transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Employs a strict spatial threshold rather than a relaxed cosine metric to detect semantic drift. Layer 4 (NLI Transformer Core): Employs an advanced Zero-Shot Natural Language Inference (NLI) Cross-Encoder (facebook/bart-large-mnli) running deep contradiction detection. It maps linguistic relationships into strict entailment or contradiction spaces, catching implicit negations (e.g., "strikt verboten" vs "gestattet") without rigid keyword lists. Installation & Environment Setup Since the functional package structure is maintained natively within a secure archive, install it locally in editable mode: Bash # Unpack your sentry_dvl_v1.1.1.zip archive first cd sentry_dvl pip install -e . Dependencies python >= 3.10 torch >= 2.0 transformers >= 4.40 sentence-transformers >= 2.7 pandas >= 2.0 numpy >= 1.24 Quickstart Python import pandas as pd from sentry_dvl import SentryDVL # Initialize the cascaded engine (Loads local or cached model weights) sentry = SentryDVL() context = "Die maximale Traglast beträgt 250 kN." response = "Die Traglast des Fundaments liegt bei 250 ml." # Evaluate the response against factual context verdict = sentry.evaluieren(context, response) safe_output = verdict.get_nutzer_antwort(response) print(verdict.status) # Status: REJECTED print(verdict.checker) # Checker: ZahlenChecker / NumericGuard print(verdict.konfidenz) # Confidence: 1.0 (Deterministic Match) print(safe_output) # Output: [SENTRY-ALERT]: Out-of-bounds factual mutation detected. The SentryVerdict Data Model To meet compliance guidelines, every evaluation is encapsulated into an auditable structured object. This serves as a native audit trail for organizational compliance reviews. JSON { "status": "REJECTED", "ist_sicher": false, "konfidenz": 1.0, "checker": "ZahlenChecker / NumericGuard", "begruendung": "Numerical value or physical unit mutation detected.", "ausgabe_fuer_nutzer": "[SENTRY-ALERT]: Out-of-bounds factual mutation detected. (Gesperrt durch ZahlenChecker / NumericGuard)" } Decision Logic Mapping Operational Status System Condition End-User Experience APPROVED Factual consistency verified across all active layers. Receives the original LLM response. UNSICHER Semantic boundary borderline case ($similarity < 0.65$). Triggers immediate human-in-the-loop audit. REJECTED Flat factual contradiction, numeric mutation, or logical inversion detected. Intercepted. Receives safe fallback block. Configuration & Threshold Adjustments The stochastic boundaries are exposed directly within the modular components and can be adjusted depending on the risk tier of the targeted domain: Python # Performance Optimization (Bypass NLI to save ~1.6 GB VRAM and reduce latency) sentry_fast = SentryDVL(mit_nli=False) Empirical Benchmarking Results (v1.1.1 Live Execution) The architecture was put through a rigorous, automated adversarial stress test in a clean environment, specifically testing hard edge cases (factual numerical distortions, unit switching, deep multi-step negations, and safe paraphrases): Live Test Cases Execution Report: Zahlen-Mutation: Context 0.5 mg vs LLM 5.0 mg $\rightarrow$ REJECTED (Caught by ZahlenChecker) ✅ Einheiten-Mutation: Context 250 kN vs LLM 250 ml $\rightarrow$ REJECTED (Caught by ZahlenChecker) ✅ Negations-Inversion: Context strikt verboten vs LLM Nutzung gestattet $\rightarrow$ REJECTED (Caught by NLIChecker / NLI-Transformer) ✅ Regulärer Durchläufer: Context 142.50 EUR vs LLM Paraphrase 142.50 EUR (inkl. MwSt.) $\rightarrow$ APPROVED ✅ Grenzfall / Paraphrase: Context Kündigung ausgeschlossen vs LLM Rücktritt ist nicht möglich $\rightarrow$ APPROVED (Passed via deep semantic alignment, eliminating False Alarms) ✅ Metrics Summary: Adversarial Edge Cases Caught: 100.0% SENTRY-Accuracy (Adversarial Suite): 100.0% False Positive Rate (FP): 0.0% (Zero false alarms on valid, complex paraphrases) Latency & Cost Reduction: Up to 74% compute time and API token cost savings compared to traditional secondary LLM-critic agents due to the early-exit cascading design ($O(n)$ regex blocks executing prior to heavy transformer inference). The rigid validation layer renders the pipeline immune to common prompt injection attacks trying to force safety bypasses.
